articles.headline: Treasury Sanctions Iranian Shadow Banking Network in Latest 'Operation Economic Outcast' Action
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has imposed sanctions on over two dozen Iranian exchange houses, front companies, and key personnel. This action, part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' aims to disrupt Iran's global shadow banking networks, which are used to circumvent sanctions and fund illicit activities.

The targeted financial infrastructure is described as underpinning much of Iran's remaining foreign trade, facilitating the movement of billions of dollars through the international financial system. OFAC's designations include Iranian exchange houses, 'rahbar companies' (offshore front companies), and the Iran Center for Exchange of Currency and Gold.

This action was taken pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 13902, which targets certain sectors of the Iranian economy, E.O. 13224, as amended, a counter-terrorism designation authority, and E.O. 13871, which targets persons operating in various sectors of Iran's metals industry.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Individuals Involved in Iranian Oil Sales; Issues New Cuba FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran designations, targeting individuals involved in facilitating Iranian oil sales and supporting previously designated entities. This action falls under 'Operation Economic Outcast,' which aims to sever economic lifelines sustaining the Iranian regime.

The designations were imposed pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 13902, which targets certain sectors of the Iranian economy, and E.O. 13224, as amended, the United States' counterterrorism sanctions authority.

In a separate but concurrent action, OFAC also issued new Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) related to Cuba sanctions. These FAQs provide guidance on existing Cuba-related restrictions and compliance considerations.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Cyber-related Designations; Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and cyber-related illicit activities. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to combat transnational criminal organizations and malicious cyber actors.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued an Illicit Drugs General License, providing authorizations for certain transactions related to illicit drug interdiction and enforcement. Additionally, an amended Russia-related General License and associated Frequently Asked Questions were released, offering updated guidance on transactions involving Russia.

The counter narcotics designations included 14 individuals and six entities tied to international narcotics trafficking, specifically targeting the Italian 'Ndrangheta and the Comanchero Outlaw Motorcycle Gang.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new counter terrorism designations. These actions target individuals and entities identified as supporting terrorist organizations and their activities globally. The specific details of the designated parties were not immediately released but are expected to be published in the Federal Register.

These designations fall under the authority of Executive Order 13224, as amended, which targets terrorists and those who provide support to terrorists or acts of terrorism. The U.S. government continues to use its sanctions authorities to disrupt the financial networks of terrorist groups.
This action underscores the ongoing commitment of the U.S. Treasury to combat global terrorism by cutting off financial resources and isolating those who facilitate such activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in both counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. This dual focus highlights the interconnectedness of illicit financial networks that often support various criminal and terrorist enterprises.

These designations aim to disrupt the financial flows and operational capabilities of organizations engaged in drug trafficking and those providing material support to terrorist groups. The specific entities and individuals targeted were not immediately detailed in the initial announcement.

This action is part of the U.S. government's broader strategy to leverage financial sanctions to protect national security and combat threats posed by international criminal and terrorist organizations.

Such updates are routine and serve to ensure the accuracy and effectiveness of the sanctions program by providing clarity to the public and financial institutions regarding sanctioned parties.
The specific nature of the update was not detailed in the brief announcement, but it is part of OFAC's ongoing efforts to maintain pressure on the Iranian regime.

articles.headline: U.S. Sanctions Cripple Financial Networks Sustaining the Iranian Regime
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations, targeting financial networks that sustain the Iranian regime. This action is part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' a broader initiative to sever economic lifelines to Iran.

These designations aim to disrupt the flow of funds and resources that the Iranian government uses to support its various activities, including those deemed destabilizing to regional and global security.
The Treasury Department emphasized its commitment to dismantling illicit networks that allow the Iranian regime to evade sanctions and fund its operations.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Cyber-related and Transnational Criminal Organizations Designations; Cuba Sanctions Expanded
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting cyber-related illicit activities and transnational criminal organizations. These actions aim to disrupt malicious cyber actors and criminal networks that pose a threat to U.S. national security and financial systems.

In a significant move, OFAC also imposed new Cuba designations and published a Cuba-related determination. These measures pave the way for sanctions on the electronics, manufacturing, marine, and technology sectors of the Cuban economy.

The U.S. government's expanded Cuba sanctions also targeted a crude oil shipping network, state-owned entities, and China-based suppliers of Cuba's military forces, according to Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian Entities, Updates Listings, and Amends Venezuela-related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations and updates to certain existing Iran-related listings. Concurrently, OFAC published an Iran-related alert, providing guidance on potential sanctions risks.

In a separate action, OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question. This amendment further delays the effectiveness of the authorization in General License 5 until December 18, 2026, impacting transactions related to the PDVSA 2020 8.5 percent bond.

The amended General License means that transactions related to the sale or transfer of CITGO shares in connection with the PDVSA 2020 8.5 percent bond are prohibited unless specifically authorized by OFAC during this period.

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Fined $11,662,930 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations

This enforcement action, which also involved a $1.2 billion FinCEN civil money penalty, underscores the severe consequences for financial institutions that fail to adequately prevent sanctions breaches and money laundering.

articles.headline: BIS Implements New Export Controls on Remote Access to Advanced U.S. AI Technology
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has issued an interim final rule, 'Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors,' effective November 19, 2026. This rule aims to prevent foreign entities from circumventing U.S. export controls by remotely accessing advanced American computing technology through data centers located in third countries.

The new regulations establish licensing requirements for exports, reexports, and transfers of advanced computing items, including advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips and servers, intended for overseas data centers that provide significant computing capacity to restricted foreign entities. This extends controls beyond the physical shipment of chips and servers to the remote provision of computing power.

The rule also introduces additional export restrictions for Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand, which BIS identifies as presenting a 'higher-than-normal risk of diversion.' Furthermore, it formally rescinds the previous AI Diffusion Rule, replacing it with more targeted restrictions on advanced computing technology.
articles.source: Federal Register / Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
